entries.answer:
Yes—your core design is the strongest scaletozero pattern when “zero idle GPU billing” matters more than absolute firstrequest latency: initialize and warm the model once, snapshot the prepared CPU/GPU process state, and restore that state rather than rebuilding the serving stack on every scaleup. This moves the recurring cost from weight loading, CUDA setup, compilation, graph capture, profiling, and allocator initialization to a much shorter snapshot restore path.[1][2]

 What snapshots solve

A conventional LLM cold start has several distinct phases:

1. Provision container and GPU.
2. Load checkpoint weights from storage into host memory and then GPU HBM.
3. Initialize vLLM/runtime structures and size KVcache pools.
4. Run warmup traffic to trigger compilation and kernel selection.
5. Capture CUDA graphs and establish steadystate execution state.
6. Accept the first production request.

For large models, checkpoint transfer is often the dominant stage; however, simply speeding up weight loading still leaves the rest of the initialization path. A GPUmemory snapshot taken after the runtime is fully warmed can skip all of those repeated stages rather than optimizing just one of them. The reported Modal/vLLM example explicitly starts vLLM, warms it, puts it into sleep mode, snapshots CPU and GPU state, then wakes it after restore so it can serve immediately.[1]

That makes the architecture materially different from:

| Approach | Avoids modelweight load? | Avoids compile/graph setup? | Ongoing idle GPU cost |
||:|:|:|
| Alwayswarm replica | Yes, while it stays alive | Yes | High |
| Fast/streaming loader | Partly reduces it | No | Zero while scaled down |
| vLLM sleep only | Depends on sleep level | Preserves some runtime state | Not a true processscaletozero solution by itself |
| Warmed GPU memory snapshot | Yes on restore path | Yes, if captured after warmup | Zero between allocated workers |

The exact restore time still depends on model size, snapshot size, storage locality, platform behavior, GPU type, and startup queueing. But the qualitative conclusion is right: snapshots eliminate the whole repeated initialization pipeline, not merely the disktoHBM component.[2][1]

 Correct snapshot boundary

Your recommendation to remove requestspecific KV state before snapshotting is important, especially with a 131ktoken context budget.

vLLM’s sleep mode is designed to release GPU memory by offloading or discarding model state and by discarding KV cache. Its documentation states that Level 1 offloads model weights to CPU RAM and discards KV cache, while Level 2 discards both weights and KV cache; in either case, KVcache contents are forgotten.[3]

The desired snapshot boundary is therefore:

 Keep: process/runtime initialization, compiled artifacts, CUDA context/runtime state where supported, graphcapture work, tokenizer/model metadata, scheduler structures, and prepared serving configuration.
 Do not snapshot: active request KV pages, old session KV blocks, scheduler queues, user prompts, transient request tensors, and other highchurn state.
 Recreate after restore: the active KVcache arena sized for the currently chosen model, max context, concurrency target, and GPUmemory utilization policy.

This avoids turning the snapshot into a serialized copy of arbitrary historical conversations. At 131k context, persistent perrequest KV data can dominate usable HBM and also makes snapshots less portable, slower, and more operationally fragile.

One nuance: discarding all KV cache before the snapshot improves restore economics, but it means the snapshot itself does not preserve peruser conversational cache hits across a true scaletozero event. That is the right tradeoff for a base image/snapshot. Preserve reusable prefixes separately in a cache tier, not inside the immutable runtime snapshot.

 Fast firsttoken layer

GPU snapshot restore fixes engine cold start. It does not eliminate prompt prefill for a newly arrived long context.

For longcontext workloads, prefill can dominate timetofirsttoken. vLLM’s Automatic Prefix Caching reuses cached KV blocks when requests share an identical prefix, allowing the shared portion to bypass recomputation.  That makes it appropriate for stable tokenidentical material such as:[4][5]

 System prompts and tool schemas.
 Tenant or workspace policies.
 Repository maps and stable project instructions.
 Pinned documents or retrieved source packs.
 Conversation turns that remain unchanged.
 Immutable filebuffer prefixes in an IDE workflow.

Predictive warming is the next layer: prefill the likely static prefix before the user sends the final request, but schedule it as interruptible lowpriority work. The production pattern described in the supplied material uses debounced UI events, document ingestion, and agentgraph signals to trigger speculative prefill; it recommends chunking speculative work and preempting it immediately for live decoding.[6]

A practical request path is:

text
Upload / file change / typing pause
        ↓
Canonicalize and tokenize stable prefix
        ↓
Hash prefix + tenant + model revision + adapter revision
        ↓
Route to deterministic worker
        ↓
Low-priority chunked speculative prefill
        ↓
Pin KV blocks briefly with a TTL
        ↓
User submits request
        ↓
Same-worker/session-affine route
        ↓
Prefix-KV hit → prefill only the delta → decode


Sessionsticky or prefixaffine routing is mandatory. A warmed prefix stranded on worker A has no direct TTFT benefit if the request is loadbalanced to worker B. Consistent hashing by session/workspace plus a canonical prefix hash is the normal solution; short TTL pinning prevents speculative work from permanently consuming HBM.[6]

 Recommended operating model

Use a threetier strategy rather than treating snapshots and KV caching as substitutes:

 Tier 0 — no workers: GPU allocation is zero; only the snapshot artifact and metadata persist.
 Tier 1 — restored base worker: restore the GPU snapshot containing a fully initialized, warmed engine but no request KV state.
 Tier 2 — activeprefix worker: keep hot reusable prefix KV blocks in GPU HBM while a worker is serving active demand; optionally use host/remote cache tiers for larger reusable caches.
 Tier 3 — optional remote KV tier: store highvalue reusable prefixes outside HBM when the network transfer cost is less than recomputing their prefill. The supplied architecture describes host DRAM and RDMAbacked cache pools as alternatives for this tier.[6]

Set separate policies for each:

| Resource | Suggested policy |
|||
| GPU runtime snapshot | Rebuild whenever model weights, runtime version, CUDA version, driver compatibility, tokenizer, quantization, adapter baseline, or graphaffecting configuration changes |
| Longlived base state | Snapshot after deliberate warmup only |
| Request KV cache | Never include in base snapshot |
| Stable global prefixes | Automatic Prefix Caching with canonical token ordering |
| Predictive prefixes | Strict quota, lowpriority chunked prefill, 10–60 second TTL, preemptible |
| Routing | Sticky by session/workspace and canonical prefix hash |
| Scaleup | Restore snapshot before admitting the waiting request whenever platform queueing allows |
| Scaledown | Drain active decode, discard perrequest KV, then terminate rather than retain an idle GPU |

 Guardrails and measurement

The approach wins only if speculative cache work is controlled. Background prefills can hurt interactive decode latency because prefill is computeintensive, so reserve capacity for live traffic and preempt speculative jobs first.[6]

Track these metrics separately:

 Restoretoready latency.
 Firstrequest TTFT after a restore.
 P50/P95/P99 TTFT split by cold restore, prefix hit, and prefix miss.
 Prefill tokens avoided through cache reuse.
 Speculativeprefill acceptance rate.
 GPU HBM utilization and eviction rate.
 Rate of session routes landing on the cacheowning worker.
 Snapshot build duration, artifact size, restore failures, and invalidation frequency.
 Cost per completed request, including speculative GPU work.

The key decision rule is simple: snapshot the reusable machine state; cache the reusable token state; discard the userspecific transient state. Snapshot restore addresses scalefromzero initialization, while prefix/KV reuse addresses longcontext prefill. Combining them is more effective than relying on either technique alone.[4][1][6]
